definition: When a soft-body mass leads a motion with one part (leading motion) and the rest trails behind, deliberately keeping the trailing material's contact point stuck/anchored to a surface a beat longer than momentum alone would dictate — rather than letting it roll or slide freely away like an inert solid (the video's own contrast: "rather than just like rolling away like Play-Doh") — communicates to the audience that the material is adhesive/sticky to the touch, purely through timing, with no additional visual detail needed.
purpose: Communicate a specific tactile material property (stickiness/adhesion) using only the timing of an existing motion (leading motion with a lagging trailer), rather than adding texture, sound, or explicit visual cues.
visible_effect: The trailing edge of a moving blob stays anchored to the ground/surface noticeably longer than its own momentum would require, then releases and catches up, rather than smoothly peeling or rolling away the instant the leading part moves.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: The audience infers a physical sensation (this would feel sticky/tacky to touch) purely from timing — the video frames this as a deliberate, general strategy: "as an animator I'm always looking for ways to let the audience know what the physical Sensations in the scene might be."
physical_interpretation: Approximates real adhesive/viscous behavior, where a material genuinely resists separating from a surface it is in contact with (surface tension, tackiness) rather than being free to slide the instant a force is applied elsewhere in its body.
use_cases: any soft-body material meant to read as sticky, viscous, or adhesive (slime, syrup, wet paint) during a leading-motion move
generally: communicating a tactile material property through timing alone rather than added visual texture
non_use_cases: a material meant to read as non-adhesive/inert (the video's own named contrast, Play-Doh) — there, the trailing part should release and roll/slide freely as soon as momentum allows, with no extra held contact
interactions: motion_path_first_volume_second_authoring_sequence (this same video) — leading motion is described as "exactly what we were doing with the magic blob earlier," i.e. the same lag/catch-up relationship between a leading point and trailing volume, here given a specific material-communication purpose

material_properties_via_spacing_alone (v10, compiled) — a closely related existing principle (material read from spacing/timing alone); this entry is a specific, concrete mechanism (an anchored trailing CONTACT POINT held longer than momentum requires) rather than spacing in general, so it is recorded as a sibling worth naming specifically rather than folded silently into the existing card
cadence_representation: Cadence's contact/constraint model (`ai/constraints.js`, `measureContactDrift`) already represents a declared contact holding a part in place for a duration — the MACHINERY for "this point stays put longer than free motion would produce" already exists for rigid rig parts and effectors. What is missing is the same soft-body volume gap as this batch's other entries: Cadence has no deforming trailing material to apply an extended contact hold to, only rigid rig parts. If a rig-based effector (a hand, a foot) were used to convey a similar adhesive read, the existing contact/hold machinery could already express the TIMING half of this technique.
control_surface: `lock_constraint`/contact markers could hold a rig effector in place for a declared duration, the closest existing analogue for the timing half of this technique on a rigid part.
detection_and_measurement_methods: `measureContactDrift` already measures how long/how firmly a declared contact holds; applying that measurement to judge whether a hold is longer than momentum alone would produce (and therefore reads as "sticky") is not something this build currently interprets — the raw measurement exists, the material-property inference from it does not.
generation_or_modification_methods: `lock_constraint` extends a contact's hold duration on a rig part; no soft-body equivalent exists.
failure_modes: letting a soft-body trailer release and move freely the instant the leading part does, losing the sticky/adhesive read entirely and defaulting to an inert-material impression
holding the contact so long it reads as the material being stuck/broken rather than merely tacky
examples: "I'm letting the trailing slime stick to the ground a little too rather than just like rolling away like Play-Doh this gives the audience a clearer idea of what the Slime might feel like to touch" (video @ 11:22–11:36)
reapplied later in the same scene: "you can see I've let it stay a bit sticky to the ground which once again adds a bit of physical sensation to the scene" (video @ 14:26–14:33)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/VjAbB9492VA @ 11:22–11:36, 14:26–14:33 — Alex Grigg names the technique and its communicative purpose explicitly, applying it twice in the same demonstration; experimental until validated
